title: Ocular coloboma—a comprehensive review for the clinician
study_design: Comprehensive narrative review of ocular coloboma. The authors examined published accounts of associated syndromes, genetic loci and chromosomal abnormalities, along with their cited references, and organized the findings by ocular involvement and inheritance pattern.
clinical_background: Typical ocular coloboma results from incomplete closure of the embryonal fissure. It may arise sporadically, be inherited, or occur with chromosomal abnormalities; systemic anomalies are more likely when chromosomal abnormalities are involved. Ocular involvement ranges from subtle defects with little functional effect to severe malformations. Vision may be reduced by involvement of the optic disc or fovea, or by complications such as retinal detachment, choroidal neovascularization and cataract. Although the congenital defect cannot be corrected, many associated complications can be treated.
objectives: To provide clinicians with a comprehensive review of ocular coloboma, including its developmental basis, clinical manifestations, complications and management.
To evaluate published information on genetic and systemic associations and organize reported colobomas by ocular involvement and inheritance pattern.
interpretation: Ocular coloboma ranges from minor defects with little functional effect to severe abnormalities. Vision may be impaired by involvement of the optic disc or fovea, or by complications including retinal detachment (RD) and choroidal neovascularisation. Genetic causes appear complex, and sporadic cases are more common; the authors consider environmental and maternal factors probable contributors to some sporadic cases, while noting that evidence for environmental causes is largely circumstantial. Identifying inter-calary membrane (ICM) detachment is central to determining whether a coloboma contributes to RD. For coloboma-related RD, pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade and laser treatment along the coloboma margin is associated with good anatomical outcomes, although visual recovery can remain limited by disc or macular involvement. Cataract surgery carries an elevated complication risk in these eyes. Complete prophylactic laser treatment may substantially reduce RD risk where it can be performed safely, but the benefit of partial treatment remains unresolved.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The cited surgical series reported anatomical success rates of 81.17% in 85 eyes in the series by Gopal et al., 88.1% in 40 eyes in the series by Pal et al., 88.9% in 46 eyes in the series by Nagpal et al., and 87.4% in a multi-centric retrospective study of 119 eyes. Despite anatomical success rates of more than 80%, the article reports visual acuity better than 20/400 in only 35.7–78.4% of cases. Earlier scleral-buckling reports had less favourable results: Jesberg and Schepens achieved reattachment in four of seven cases, while Wang reported success in six of the fourteen eyes treated with a figure-of-eight buckle and one of the six eyes treated with a conventional buckle. In the cited prophylactic-laser study by Tripathi et al., two of 201 treated eyes developed RD during 3 years of follow-up; the authors state that this and the shorter follow-up reported by Uhumwangho et al. do not establish laser efficacy because RD risk accumulates with age.
clinical_implications: Optic disc and foveal involvement can limit vision independently of complications and help explain why anatomical RD repair does not always produce comparable functional recovery.
Even a narrow area of ICM detachment indicates that the coloboma contributes to RD; detecting it matters when distinguishing coloboma-related RD from detachment caused by a peripheral lesion.
A small cornea does not necessarily indicate a small eyeball, and ectasia within a coloboma can make an ultrasound measurement of eye size falsely normal or larger than normal.

Incomplete laser coverage can leave a communication between the sub-ICM and sub-retinal spaces untreated. In many eyes, optic disc involvement makes safe treatment of the entire coloboma margin difficult.
Microphthalmos and relatively hard lenses can make cataract surgery more difficult and increase intra-operative risk.
practice_implications: For an apparently isolated uveal coloboma, Huynh et al. suggest physical examination, baseline audiology assessment, kidney ultrasound and spine X-ray.
Assess whether ICM detachment is present when planning RD treatment. If the coloboma's contribution remains uncertain, the authors advise assuming that it contributes.
A peripheral scleral buckle can be chosen for RD confidently judged unrelated to the coloboma; a pars plana vitrectomy approach is used in most other situations.

During vitrectomy for coloboma-related RD, the authors recommend triamcinolone to help induce PVD and advise treating the entire coloboma margin with laser because the precise site of communication is usually unknown and PVD induction can create additional tears.

Laser treatment near a fovea adjacent to the coloboma margin may require sparing the fovea. Where the optic disc is involved, the authors advise carefully applied light burns along its functional border to avoid nerve fibre layer injury; they note that diode laser can help avoid full-thickness burns.

The authors consider long-term silicone oil tamponade desirable in most coloboma-related RD cases, while C3F8 may be acceptable in selected cases. When using silicone oil, they indicate that 5000 centistokes may be preferable.
At silicone oil removal, carefully evaluate the whole retina, including the coloboma margin, so that an identified problem can be addressed during the same procedure.

For cataract surgery, Kohli et al. recommend phaco emulsification for softer cataracts when corneal diameter is >8 mm and M-SICS for smaller corneas with hard nuclear cataracts. The article also reports a recommendation for a pars plana approach in extremely microphthalmic eyes, even with hard lenses.

For prophylactic laser to be effective, the authors state that the whole coloboma margin must be surrounded by at least 2–3 rows of burns; they consider this safely achievable only when the coloboma does not involve the disc or macula and sufficient space separates its margin from both.
limitations: The authors identify a gap in Ida Mann’s classification: it does not specify how the optic disc itself is affected when it lies within a choroidal coloboma.
The authors identify a gap in the classification by Gopal et al.: it does not account for an isolated coloboma at the optic nerve entrance.
The cited prophylactic-laser studies have follow-up too short to determine efficacy against an RD risk that increases with age.
open_questions: Whether partial prophylactic laser treatment of the coloboma margin reduces RD risk remains unanswered without long-term studies.
The ideal internal tamponade for coloboma-related RD has not been established.
future_directions: Improve identification of the causes of non-syndromic coloboma.
Develop better swept source OCT imaging with longer scans to provide a panoramic view of the anatomy.
Conduct randomized controlled trials of prophylactic laser photocoagulation for RD prevention.
Conduct randomized controlled trials to determine the ideal internal tamponade for coloboma-related RD.

main_findings.description: The review describes ocular coloboma as a consequence of incomplete embryonal fissure closure, with presentations ranging from subtle ocular changes to a nonfunctional eye associated with an orbital cyst.
main_findings.context: Coloboma affecting the optic disc or fovea can impair vision; retinal detachment, choroidal neovascularization, cataract and amblyopia can cause additional visual loss.

main_findings.description: The genetic basis of coloboma appears complex, and the reported phenotype varies substantially without correlating with genotype.
main_findings.context: The review describes isolated sporadic or familial disease, syndromic disease, and a greater likelihood of systemic abnormalities when chromosomal aberrations are involved.

main_findings.description: The MAC study did not identify pathogenic mutations in PAX6, CHX10 or SIX3 among patients with fundus coloboma.
main_findings.context: Result attributed to the MAC study.

main_findings.description: A separate study found no PAX6 mutations among patients with fundus coloboma.
main_findings.context: Result attributed to the cited study.

main_findings.description: CHARGE syndrome was reported among a proportion of people with coloboma.
main_findings.context: The review presents this as an association reported in the literature.

main_findings.description: In Shah et al.'s study, systemic features were more common with bilateral than unilateral AMC.
main_findings.context: AMC denotes Anophthalmia, microphthalmos, coloboma in the article.

main_findings.description: Huynh et al. detected abnormalities through systemic investigations of patients whose uveal coloboma had appeared isolated; most detected abnormalities did not call for urgent intervention.
main_findings.context: The investigations included echocardiography, renal ultrasound, audiology, spine X-ray and brain MRI.

main_findings.description: The iris can be involved in fundus coloboma, but iris involvement is neither obligatory nor correlated with the severity of the fundus defect.
The optic-disc configuration associated with the choroidal coloboma was related to coloboma size and visual outcome in the classification by Gopal et al.
main_findings.context: Type 5 was the commonest configuration; large choroidal defects and poor vision occurred more often in types 4–6.

main_findings.description: OCT can identify a communication between the sub-retinal and sub-ICM spaces at Locus minoris resistantiae when ICM is detached.
main_findings.context: Even a narrow rim of ICM detachment indicates that the coloboma contributes to a retinal detachment. A taut ICM can also produce shallow detachment beyond the coloboma border.

main_findings.description: ICG angiography demonstrated an absence of choroiocapillaris within the coloboma and in neighboring areas of chorio retinal atrophy.
main_findings.context: Retinal vessels supplying tissue beyond the defect may cross the coloboma and may be partly concealed within ectatic sclera.

main_findings.description: Published hospital-based studies reported a broad range of retinal-detachment prevalence in chorio-retinal coloboma.
main_findings.context: The review states that population prevalence of coloboma-related retinal detachment is unknown.

main_findings.description: A cited estimate indicated that the odds of retinal detachment increased with each additional year.

main_findings.context: Estimate attributed to the cited study.

main_findings.description: An isolated ICM break can detach the ICM without producing retinal detachment beyond the coloboma; a communication at Locus minoris resistantiae can instead allow fluid to extend into the surrounding retina.
main_findings.context: The review describes combined ICM breaks and dehiscence at Locus minoris resistantiae as perhaps the commonest mechanism of coloboma-related retinal detachment.

main_findings.context: Among 46 eyes, 38 eyes underwent vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade and 8 eyes underwent scleral buckling.

main_findings.description: A multicentric retrospective study reported final anatomical success after treatment of coloboma-related retinal detachment.
main_findings.context: Study of 119 eyes; tamponade was silicone oil in 77.3% eyes, SF6 in 10.1% and C3F8 in 12.6%.

main_findings.description: In the multicentric retrospective study, SF6 tamponade was associated with recurrent retinal detachment.
main_findings.context: This result pertains to the eyes receiving SF6.

main_findings.description: The review reports a range of eyes attaining visual acuity better than the specified threshold despite anatomical success rates exceeding the specified level.
main_findings.metric: proportion with visual acuity better than 20/400
main_findings.context: The article describes anatomical success rates of more than 80% and attributes the difference between anatomical and visual outcomes to optic-disc and macular involvement.

main_findings.description: Subfoveal CNV has been reported when the macula lies near the margin of a choroidal coloboma.
main_findings.context: Reported approaches included laser photocoagulation, photodynamic therapy with Verteporfin, anti VEGF injections and surgical removal.

main_findings.description: Mohamed et al. identified cataract in eyes from a series of patients with uveal coloboma.
main_findings.context: Series of 145 eyes of 98 patients, with a mean age of 23 years.

main_findings.description: Mohamed et al. identified nuclear sclerosis as the commonest lens opacity.
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to Mohamed et al.'s series.

main_findings.description: Mohamed et al. observed a linear opacity at the coloboma site, which they called ‘coloboma cataract’.
main_findings.metric: proportion of cases with linear opacity
main_findings.context: Finding attributed to Mohamed et al.'s series.

main_findings.description: Tripathi et al. observed retinal detachment despite prophylactic laser in treated eyes with choroidal coloboma.
main_findings.context: The report involved 201 eyes followed for 3 years; in three of four treatment patterns, portions of the margin were left untreated to protect the macula.

main_findings.description: Uhumwangho et al. reported different mean follow-up durations for treatment-naïve and laser-treated patients.
main_findings.value: 1.59 years in treatment naïve patients vs. 0.79 years in lasertreated patient
main_findings.context: The review states that the short follow-up in this and Tripathi et al.'s study does not establish the efficacy of prophylactic laser.

notable_adverse_events: In Gopal et al.'s series of coloboma-related retinal detachments, raised intraocular pressure was reported in 16% of eyes.
Chaurasia et al. reported intra-operative complications in 8/26 eyes undergoing cataract surgery; these included rhexis extension, posterior capsular rupture and vitreous loss.
Phylactou et al. reported posterior capsular tear with vitreous loss in 19.5% of cataract operations.
Kohli et al. reported complications after phaco emulsification or manual small incisional cataract surgery (MSICS) in 9.3% of a series of 280 eyes with coloboma and cataract.

The review describes a potential risk of nerve fibre layer damage from heavy laser burns near the functional optic-disc border and a potential risk of foveal injury from broad laser treatment when the fovea is close to the coloboma margin.
The review notes that delaying silicone oil removal can increase the risk of oil-induced complications.

tables.title: Table 4. Glossary of terms related to systemic abnormalities associated with fundus coloboma

rows: Partial or complete failure of development of the structure connecting the cerebral hemispheres.
Permanent bending of one or more fingers.
A manifestation within the holoprosencephaly spectrum, with a single nostril lacking a septum and separate, closely spaced eyes.
Brain tissue extends into the spinal canal. Type 1 arises during brain and skull growth and is therefore acquired, unlike the congenital and more severe types 2 and 3.
Soft tissue or bone narrows or obstructs the posterior nasal cavity, causing breathing difficulty.
Narrowing of a portion of the aorta.
Early closure of one or more skull-bone joints.
Partial or complete failure of development of the cerebellar vermis joining the cerebellar hemispheres.
Abnormal bodily structure encompassing malformation from abnormal development, dysplasia from disordered tissue growth or organisation, and deformation from an external force.
Sac-like extension of brain and its membranes through a skull opening.
Abnormal smallness of one side of the face; microsomia denotes unusually small body structures.
Failure of the prosencephalon, which forms the forebrain, to divide into two hemispheres.
Congenital megacolon resulting from missing ganglion cells.

Unilateral or bilateral hypopigmentation following lines of Blaschko, which reflect normal embryonic skin-cell migration and become visible in disease; examples include a ‘V’ on the back, ‘S’-shaped whorls on the chest and sides, and waves on the head.
Spinal curvature in both the side-to-side and front-to-back planes.
Absent or diminished normal brain convolutions.
Head size greater than 2 standard deviations above the age- and sex-specific norm; possible causes include hydrocephalus or megalencephaly associated with metabolic disorders or neurofibromatosis.
A skull longer than expected in relation to its width.
Colonic dilation that is not due to obstruction.
Head size more than two standard deviations below the age- and sex-specific norm.
Brain gyri that are fewer, wider and flatter.
An additional finger beside the little finger (ulnar side) or toe beside the little toe (lateral side).
An additional finger beside the thumb (radial side) or toe beside the great toe (medial side).
Soft-tissue fusion of adjacent fingers, with or without fused bone.
Short distal phalanges with cone-shaped epiphyses.
Spastic paralysis affecting all four limbs.
Early fusion of the metopic suture between the frontal bones, restricting transverse growth and producing a triangular skull.

main_conclusion: Ocular coloboma varies widely in presentation and may reduce vision directly through disc or foveal involvement or through complications. Recognising ICM detachment helps determine whether a retinal detachment is coloboma-related; the authors report good surgical success with pars plana vitrectomy, silicone oil tamponade and endolaser at the coloboma margin, while noting an increased complication risk during cataract surgery.
narrative_summary:
This comprehensive clinical review examines the development, genetics, systemic associations, ocular manifestations and management of ocular coloboma. Defective embryonal fissure closure causes typical coloboma, but presentation ranges from subtle iris defects to a non-functional eye with an orbital cyst. Coloboma may be isolated, familial or associated with chromosomal abnormalities; the authors note that systemic abnormalities are more likely with chromosomal aberrations. Vision depends particularly on optic disc and foveal involvement and may deteriorate through retinal detachment, choroidal neovascularisation or cataract.

Hospital-based studies cited in the review report retinal detachment prevalence ranging from 2.4 to 47.5%. For a detached retina, identifying even limited ICM detachment is important evidence that the coloboma contributes to its cause. The authors favour a pars plana approach with treatment of the coloboma margin and describe silicone oil as desirable for long-term tamponade in most cases. Cited surgical series reported anatomical success rates of 81.17%, 88.1%, 88.9% and 87.4%, although visual outcomes were less consistently favourable when the disc or macula was affected. Cataract surgery carries an elevated complication risk in these eyes. Prophylactic laser could reduce detachment risk when complete treatment is feasible, but disc or macular proximity often limits safe coverage, and the cited studies’ follow-up does not establish its efficacy. The authors call for research into non-syndromic causes, improved imaging and randomized trials of prophylactic laser and internal tamponade.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Typical ocular coloboma results from incomplete embryonal fissure closure. It may occur sporadically, be inherited through known or unidentified genetic defects, or accompany chromosomal abnormalities; systemic abnormalities are more frequent with the chromosomal forms. Ocular involvement ranges from a barely recognizable, nonfunctional eye compressed by an orbital cyst to a minor defect with little structural or functional effect. Fundus lesions differ in their anteroposterior and transverse extent and in whether they involve the optic disc or fovea. Vision may be impaired by disc or foveal involvement, retinal detachment, choroidal neovascular membrane, cataract, or amblyopia associated with uncorrected refractive error. Although the congenital defect itself cannot be reversed, many complications can be treated substantially. Contemporary surgery for coloboma-related retinal detachment has produced consistently good outcomes. Cataract surgery can be difficult because microphthalmos may coexist with relatively hard lenses, increasing intra-operative risk. Laser retinopexy around a choroidal coloboma is a potentially useful preventive measure, but complete safe treatment is difficult when the optic disc lies within the lesion, as it does in a majority of eyes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Coloboma derives from a Greek term for mutilation. A typical fundus coloboma occupies the inferior or infero-nasal fundus and reflects failed embryonal fissure closure; comparable defects elsewhere are termed atypical. Complete involvement can affect the optic disc, choroid and retina, ciliary body, zonules, lens, and iris. At one extreme, a cyst arising at the defect can extend into the orbit and leave the eye nonfunctional; at the other, slight iris hypoplasia or a pupillary-border notch may leave function intact. Fundus coloboma can occur with varying microphthalmos. Sporadic cases are common, although systemic associations and syndromes are recognized, with genetic loci identified for some. Disc or macular involvement threatens sight, as does the lifetime risk of retinal detachment (RD). Pars plana vitrectomy has changed treatment of coloboma-related RD and now provides reproducibly good results.

document_sections.heading: Relevant embryology
document_sections.content: The eye field is specified in the medial anterior neural plate shortly after gastrulation in the 3rd week of gestation. Optic vesicles bud from the forebrain, while adjacent surface ectoderm forms the lens placode and subsequently the lens vesicle. The distal optic vesicle gives rise to neural retina, and its proximal portion gives rise to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Invagination creates the double-layered optic cup: its inner layer forms neural retina and its outer layer forms RPE. A ventral embryonal/choroidal/foetal fissure along the cup and stalk permits mesenchymal entry and normally closes by 5–7 weeks of gestation, around the 17-mm stage. Eye development requires different combinations of transcription factors, including PAX6, SIX3, LHX2, and RAX, at successive stages. Intrinsic transcription factors interact with external signalling. Optic-vesicle stem cells can form neuro-sensory retina, RPE, or optic stalk according to those signals. Prospective neural retina expresses VSX2, prospective RPE expresses MITF, and prospective optic stalk expresses PAX2. Antagonism between MITF and VSX2 establishes the RPE–neural retina boundary; antagonism between PAX2 and PAX6 defines the optic stalk–neural retina boundary. Extrinsic influences include transforming growth factor (TGFβ), fibroblast growth factor, sonic hedgehog (SHH), and WNT signalling.

document_sections.heading: Genetics and coloboma
document_sections.content: Inherited or chromosomally associated coloboma may be accompanied by systemic anomalies. The Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man resource emphasizes genotype–phenotype relationships. This review evaluated associations reported by Gregory-Evans et al., Chang et al., and their cited sources; Tables 1 and 2 organize familial and chromosomal associations. Reports describing choroidal or retinal coloboma were grouped as chorio-retinal coloboma, with separate categories for isolated iris, isolated optic disc, and chorio-retinal involvement, and associations were also organized by inheritance. Mutation screening of genes associated with embryonal-fissure development has yielded limited results: the MAC study found no pathogenic PAX6, CHX10, or SIX3 mutations in patients with fundus coloboma, and another study found no PAX6 mutation among 30 patients. The genetic basis appears complex. Coloboma may be isolated or systemic; chromosomal aberrations make systemic involvement more likely. Numerous associated genes reflect the complexity of fissure development and closure. Phenotype varies markedly without corresponding to genotype. Isolated cases may be sporadic or familial with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked inheritance. Several syndromes are associated, most commonly CHARGE syndrome; CHD7 has been identified for that syndrome, although its gene product's precise function remains unknown. SHH gene, PAX2, PAX6, and VAX genes participate in fissure formation and closure, but not every carrier of mutations in these genes develops coloboma, and additional associated genes are reported.

document_sections.heading: Sporadic coloboma
document_sections.content: Possible explanations for sporadic disease include an environmental intra-uterine insult, a genetic cause with low penetrance or expressivity, or genetic susceptibility triggered by an environmental factor. Evidence implicating environmental causes is largely circumstantial. Proposed maternal or environmental factors include Vitamin A deficiency, diabetes, hypothyroidism, alcohol use, and exposure to thalidomide, carbamazepine, or hydantoin. Experiments in rats and mice have produced offspring with coloboma after exposure during pregnancy to retinoic acid, saccharine, irradiation, or folate deficiency.

document_sections.heading: Systemic disorders and coloboma
document_sections.content: Table 3 groups reported systemic associations by organ system, while Table 4 defines associated terms that may be unfamiliar to ophthalmologists. Fifteen to thirty percent of colobomas may occur with CHARGE syndrome. Shah et al. reported that systemic features in United Kingdom patients with AMC (Anophthalmia, microphthalmos, coloboma) were more common in bilateral cases. Among 99 patients with apparently isolated uveal coloboma, Huynh et al. identified abnormalities using echocardiography, renal ultrasound, audiology, spinal X-ray, and brain MRI; most findings did not warrant urgent intervention. For apparently isolated uveal coloboma, those investigators suggested physical examination, baseline audiology, kidney ultrasound, and spinal X-ray.

document_sections.heading: Presenting symptoms
document_sections.content: Most cases are detected because parents or a paediatrician notice an abnormal-looking eye, such as a visibly small globe, marked nystagmus, strabismus, or an evident iris defect. Persistent poor vision can arise without RD through uncorrected refractive error, amblyopia, or foveal involvement and may become apparent when schooling begins. Acute visual deterioration, with or without pre-existing impairment, is most commonly due to newly occurring RD; sub foveal choroidal neovascular membrane is another possible cause. In children, visual disability may first be recognized when both eyes are affected, with an established RD in one and a more recent RD in the other; deterioration superimposed on poor baseline vision can be difficult for parents to detect. Small lesions sparing the disc and fovea may cause no symptoms unless RD develops. A large lesion can produce a yellow or white pupillary reflex, while a complicated cataract may also prompt recognition of an ocular problem.

document_sections.heading: Clinical features
document_sections.content: Involvement may be unilateral, reported in 33–47.5% of cases, or bilateral; bilateral findings may be symmetric or asymmetric.

document_sections.heading: Nystagmus
document_sections.content: When macular involvement impairs central fixation in both eyes, nystagmus may be the initial manifestation. These eyes are often substantially microphthalmic.

document_sections.heading: Anterior vs. posterior segment involvement
document_sections.content: Nakamura's study reported isolated anterior-segment involvement of the iris and ciliary body in 36%, isolated posterior-segment involvement of the chorio retinal tissues and optic nerve in 39%, and combined involvement in 24% of cases.

document_sections.heading: Microphthalmos and microcornea
document_sections.content: Corneal diameter does not invariably indicate globe size: a microphthalmic eye has a correspondingly small cornea, but microcornea can occur in a normally sized eye. Ultrasonography, CT, or MRI permits more accurate assessment of globe size. The stated age-adjusted criterion for a microphthalmic eye is an axial diameter <95th percentile. In adults and children >13 years age, an axial diameter <18.5 mm is considered microphthalmic.

document_sections.heading: Caveat
document_sections.content: Because the colobomatous area is often ectatic, an ultrasound measurement through it may falsely suggest a normal or larger-than-normal globe. This matters particularly when an extensive defect occupies much of the posterior pole.

document_sections.heading: Microphthalmos with orbital cyst
document_sections.content: Neuroectodermal hyperplasia can evert the inner layer at the embryonal-fissure edge and interfere with closure. If retinal differentiation has not occurred, closure may still produce an ectatic coloboma with ICM; after retinal differentiation, failed fusion can produce a true orbital cyst. Cysts vary in size and can become large enough to resemble an orbital tumour. In severe cases, the globe is profoundly microphthalmic or clinically almost unrecognizable because the cyst displaces it sideways or posteriorly. Communication between cyst and vitreous cavity varies. Most such eyes are nonfunctional, have dysplastic retina, and are managed with cosmesis as the objective.

document_sections.heading: Iris coloboma
document_sections.content: Iris involvement commonly accompanies fundus coloboma but is neither obligatory nor predictive of fundus-lesion severity. A complete iris defect is infero-nasal, continuous with the pupil, and gives a keyhole appearance. Partial involvement may present as a sphincter notch, pigment-epithelium defect, or heterochromia. Unlike traumatic defects, coloboma has smooth edges.

document_sections.heading: Ciliary body coloboma
document_sections.content: Ciliary muscle and pigment epithelium are absent within the affected area. Ciliary-body involvement commonly accompanies iris coloboma. Local absence of zonules consequently distorts the lens equator.

document_sections.heading: Choroidal coloboma
document_sections.content: Fundus involvement is the visually important component; severity descriptions chiefly concern the lesion's relationship to the optic disc and macula. Choroid and RPE are missing within the defect, and variable thinning of its scleral floor may cause ectasia. Its inner surface consists of exposed sclera, sometimes with pigment near the boundary, and may be smooth or scalloped. Anteroposterior extent ranges from isolated patches along the disc-to-inferior or infero-nasal periphery axis to a lesion extending into the periphery. Transverse extent generally increases with anteroposterior extent; the largest lesions can occupy almost the entire inferior fundus and tend to have greater disc involvement. Bridge coloboma denotes separate colobomatous patches with intervening normal retina.

document_sections.heading: The optic disc and the choroidal coloboma
document_sections.content: Disc involvement is anatomically varied. Classifications address both whether the disc lies inside or outside the choroidal lesion and whether disc tissue itself is colobomatous.

document_sections.heading: Classification
document_sections.content: In Ida Mann’s classification, type 1 extends above the disc, type 2 reaches its superior border, type 3 extends below its inferior border, type 4 affects only the disc, type 5 lies below the disc with normal retina both above and below the lesion, type 6 has peripheral pigmentation, and type 7 affects only the periphery. The ordering generally runs from greatest severity at type 1 to least at types 6 and 7: type 1 is expected to have the poorest vision and type 7 normal vision. Type 4 represents isolated disc disease, whereas type 5 describes a small mid-fundus lesion with normal retina anteriorly and posteriorly. This scheme does not specify how a disc situated inside choroidal coloboma is affected. Gopal et al. classify eyes into six types according to disc location and appearance. In types 1–3 the choroidal lesion does not reach the disc: type 1 has an apparently normal disc, although flattening of its inferior edge is frequent; type 2 has a dysplastic disc; and type 3 has an independently colobomatous disc outside the choroidal lesion, with either eccentric involvement or an appearance resembling glaucomatous cupping. In types 4–6 the disc lies within the choroidal lesion: type 4 retains an apparently normal disc, whereas types 5 and 6 have disc coloboma continuous with choroidal coloboma. Type 6 has the most severe loss of recognizable disc tissue. Type 5 is the commonest arrangement and retains visible creamy-pink disc tissue superiorly. Large choroidal lesions and poor vision were more frequent in types 4–6. Isolated coloboma at the optic-nerve entrance is not addressed by this classification.

document_sections.heading: The transition zone between coloboma and normal fundus
document_sections.content: The lesion boundary has features relevant to RD. At the margin, the ending RPE adheres to outer retinal layers; beyond it, retinal layers become the fibrotic inter-calary membrane (ICM). This adhesion zone, called ‘Locus minoris resistantiae’, is the point of least resistance. Photoreceptors can turn back toward the ending RPE and produce a double photoreceptor layer. The retinal-to-ICM transition may be gradual or abrupt. With pronounced ectasia, the protruding border can turn inward. Taut ICM may pull on adjacent retina and produce a shallow RD beyond the visible margin, best appreciated with optical coherence tomography (OCT). Pigmentation and chorio retinal atrophy outside the visible border vary. In RD caused by coloboma, ICM elevation varies; even a narrow detached rim supports a causal contribution from the lesion. When ICM is detached, OCT can demonstrate a defect in the zone of least resistance connecting sub-retinal and sub-ICM spaces.

document_sections.heading: Blood vessels in the coloboma
document_sections.content: Casper, as cited by Duke Elder, described three patterns of disc-vessel emergence. Most commonly, vessels leave the inferior portion of a colobomatous disc: vessels supplying inferior fundus bend sharply over the edge, whereas those supplying superior fundus pass across its excavation. Alternatively, vessels arise in a relatively normal arrangement near the disc centre, or they emerge from its edge and resemble cilio-retinal vessels. Studies comparing angiography and fundus photographs identify four vessel categories within coloboma: retinal vessels visibly continuous with disc vessels; vessels emerging from the defect whose connection with the central retinal artery or its branches can nevertheless be established; vessels arising from the defect that may be cilio-retinal; and broad, deep scleral vessels presumed to be extra ocular vessels visible through thin sclera. ICG angiography shows no choroiocapillaris within the defect or neighboring chorio retinal atrophic patches. Vessels supplying normal retina beyond the lesion can remain in normal retina or cross the defect. A crossing vessel may be entirely visible in ICM or partly concealed in ectatic sclera. Retinal vessels branch little while traversing ICM and resume usual branching after leaving the defect.

document_sections.heading: Inter-calary membrane breaks
document_sections.content: A detached ICM may contain visible breaks despite the poor contrast caused by absent choroid and RPE. Three patterns are described: oval breaks with elevation of all edges; a crescent-shaped break along the lesion border with elevation only of ICM peripheral to the break; and breaks in a macula incorporated into the coloboma.

document_sections.heading: Forme fruste lesions
document_sections.content: Incomplete manifestations include an infero-nasal iris-sphincter notch or a pigment defect visible by transillumination. Fundus findings may include posterior dipping of the infero-nasal ora serrata, chorio retinal atrophic patches, or RPE defects along the axis from disc to infero-nasal periphery. Alone, these changes are not diagnostic; their relationship to coloboma can be inferred when clearer accompanying features are present. OCT shows these fundus lesions to be mildly ectatic with comparatively preserved retinal architecture. A small true coloboma instead shows a moderately reflective membrane without identifiable retinal architecture.

document_sections.heading: Congenital cavitary optic disc anomaly (CODA)
document_sections.content: The article gives a brief account, rather than a detailed review, of cavitary disc entities and their possible relationship to embryonal closure. Isolated optic disc cavitary anomalies comprise conditions definitely attributable to defective fissure closure, conditions definitely unrelated to it, and conditions of uncertain origin. Listed entities are optic disc coloboma, morning glory syndrome, optic pit, peripapillary staphyloma, and Pedler’s coloboma. Their distinct meanings have sometimes been obscured by interchangeable terminology in the literature.

document_sections.heading: Condition definitely related to defective closure of embryonal fissure
document_sections.content: Typical optic disc coloboma can be recognized without accompanying choroidal disease by a sharply bounded, bowl-shaped excavation in the inferior disc, although some lesions resemble glaucomatous cupping. Unlike morning glory syndrome, it lacks a central glial tuft. Disc vessels are essentially normal apart from displacement by the defect. Its cause is defective closure of the proximal embryonal fissure.

document_sections.heading: Condition not related to defective closure of embryonal fissure
document_sections.content: In peripapillary staphyloma, an apparently normal disc sits at the base of an excavation produced by outward bulging of the ocular wall. Some appearances can be mistaken for colobomatous disc tissue, but inspection distinguishes the normal disc. Pigment changes often surround or line the excavation, and contractile staphylomas have been reported. Incomplete scleral differentiation from neural crest and a large scleral canal have been proposed as causes of reduced peripapillary scleral support. Swept source OCT has shown deep excavation without an internal glial membrane or tissue and normal retina beyond it.

document_sections.heading: Conditions of unsure origin
document_sections.content: Morning glory syndrome has a funnel-shaped fundus excavation containing the disc, rather than an excavation within the disc itself. Peripapillary pigment changes and atrophy accompany a central white glial tuft that appears to draw retina inward. Disc vessels are unusually numerous and relatively straight. OCT has demonstrated a defined pre-retinal membrane attached to vitreous that pulls retina centrally and prevents retinal excavation unless posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) occurs or vitreous is surgically removed. Secondary RD is common and can substantially impair sight; slit-like breaks over the disc can cause rhegmatogenous RD. The condition is predominantly unilateral, occurs more frequently in females, has widely varying presenting acuity, and has been reported with transsphenoidal encephalocele.

document_sections.heading: Pedler’s coloboma
document_sections.content: Reported cases feature an apparent mass produced by peripapillary retinal traction toward the disc, together with weakened and ectatic sclera. Defective scleral maturation is proposed as the cause. Some eyes were enucleated after the lesion was mistaken for an optic disc neoplasm. Histopathology instead found gliotic retinal tissue and a thick fold displacing the cribriform plate and disc posteriorly, with choroid prolapsing through the defect into the optic nerve sheath.

document_sections.heading: Optic disc pit
document_sections.content: Whether optic disc pit reflects defective embryonal fissure closure remains disputed. Coexistence with choroidal coloboma supports a connection: Brown and Augsburger reported nasal pits with retinochoroidal coloboma; Singerman and Mittra described optic pits and iris coloboma across three generations; and Gopal et al. described a temporal pit with inferior forme fruste lesions in one eye and typical retinochoroidal coloboma in the other. Conversely, the usual temporal rather than infero-nasal pit location weighs against this explanation. Serous macular detachment and intra-retinal fluid are common complications and can cause enduring visual impairment. Vitreous fluid and cerebro-spinal fluid have both been proposed as sources. Reported management options include observation, laser at the temporal disc border, vitrectomy with fluid air exchange, an internal limiting membrane flap intended to close the pit, and inner retinal fenestration.

document_sections.heading: Macular coloboma
document_sections.content: A macular coloboma is thought not to result from abnormal embryonal fissure closure. It appears as a variably sized oval or circular area of chorio retinal atrophy, with centrally visible white sclera and variable peripheral pigment. A bilateral example with medullated nerve fibres is shown. Reported associations include genetic disorders, congenital amaurosis of Leber and other retinal dystrophies, and congenital toxoplasmosis. On OCT, congenital developmental lesions lack retina and choroid entirely at the scar centre. Congenital toxoplasmosis instead shows retinal thinning, RPE hyper-reflectivity, excavation, intra-retinal cysts, and fibrosis.

document_sections.heading: RD and choroidal coloboma
document_sections.content: RD is the principal complication of choroidal coloboma. Its population prevalence in chorio-retinal coloboma is unknown; hospital studies report 2.4 to 47.5%. One estimate found RD odds rising by a factor of 1.147 with each additional year and falling by 0.653 with each upward step in Ida Mann classification. Here, RD means separation of normal neuro-sensory retina outside the coloboma from RPE, whereas ICM detachment means elevation of that membrane from the lesion floor. Possible dehiscences, alone or together, are peripheral retinal breaks, ICM breaks, and breaks in Locus minoris resistantiae; their combinations determine whether retinal and ICM detachment occur.

document_sections.heading: Isolated breaks in ICM
document_sections.content: An ICM break alone can detach the membrane without extension past the coloboma border. Such detachment causes no symptoms and is not uncommon in the fellow eye of a patient presenting with symptoms in one eye. Its substantial risk of progressing to clinical RD could make it an important indication for preventive laser retinopexy.

document_sections.heading: Isolated breaks in peripheral retina
document_sections.content: A peripheral break alone produces RD resembling that in an eye without coloboma: detachment ends at the coloboma boundary and ICM stays attached. Assessment must nevertheless exclude even a narrow rim of ICM detachment.

document_sections.heading: Isolated breaks in Locus minoris resistantiae
document_sections.content: An isolated defect at this site is hypothetical and, even if it occurs, would have no clinical importance.

document_sections.heading: Breaks in peripheral retina and Locus minoris resistantiae
document_sections.content: Only the peripheral retinal break is identifiable, but RD accompanies ICM detachment of variable extent.

document_sections.heading: Breaks in ICM and Locus minoris resistantiae
document_sections.content: This is perhaps the most frequent mechanism of coloboma-related RD. A defect in Locus minoris resistantiae links the sub-ICM and sub-retinal spaces, permitting clinical RD; ICM detachment of variable extent is always present.

document_sections.heading: Breaks in ICM, Locus minoris resistantiae and peripheral retinal breaks
document_sections.content: The mechanism resembles that involving ICM and the zone of least resistance, with an additional peripheral retinal break.

document_sections.heading: RD unrelated to coloboma
document_sections.content: When RD occurs in an eye with choroidal coloboma, determining whether the defect contributes is necessary to choose management. Detachment that does not cross the lesion border probably arises from a peripheral lesion. Assessment may be difficult if ICM detachment is shallow and limited to the coloboma edge, nystagmus is present, or severe microphthalmos impedes fundus examination. If the cause remains uncertain, the advised approach is to assume that coloboma contributes.

document_sections.heading: Acute vs. chronic vs. acute on chronic RD
document_sections.content: RD may be acute, chronic, or newly worsened on a chronic background. Retina immediately outside the coloboma may show longstanding detachment through thinning and RPE changes while more distant detached retina appears recently affected. Chronic detachment shows varying PVR, retinal thinning, and subretinal gliosis.

document_sections.heading: Sub-clinical RD
document_sections.content: Traction from a taut ICM can cause shallow retinal detachment immediately beyond the lesion edge. It may escape clinical examination and is best detected using OCT.

document_sections.heading: Management of RD in eyes with coloboma of choroid
document_sections.content: Vitreo retinal surgical advances have altered treatment. Vitrectomy has replaced earlier scleral-buckling approaches in most circumstances. A small number of reports describe successful pneumatic retinopexy in selected cases.

document_sections.heading: Pneumatic retinopexy
document_sections.content: Isolated reports describe retinal reattachment using pneumatic retinopexy followed by laser photocoagulation at the coloboma border. The technique is considered suitable only for very selected cases with a highly compliant patient.

document_sections.heading: Pars plana approach
document_sections.content: Vitrectomy permits direct, magnified examination of the lesion, including identification of a small detached ICM rim or membrane breaks. It allows controlled laser treatment at the coloboma edge and prolonged internal tamponade while firm marginal adhesion develops. Gonvers first reported successful vitrectomy with silicone oil for coloboma-related RD after buckling of a more evident peripheral break had failed.

document_sections.heading: Scleral buckling
document_sections.content: Historically, scleral buckling gave poor results: Jesberg and Schepens achieved reattachment in four of seven cases. Recognition of the coloboma border's importance led to radially convergent buckles, called Chinese figure of eight scleral buckles. In Wang's series, reattachment succeeded in six of the fourteen eyes receiving this configuration versus only one of the six receiving conventional buckles. Buckling cannot adequately support the posterior-most lesion or readily close ICM breaks: breaks are difficult to find in thin membrane, and absent underlying choroid and RPE prevent cryo from producing adhesion. Marked microphthalmos adds technical difficulty. Nevertheless, peripheral scleral buckle can be preferred for RD confidently determined to be unrelated to coloboma. Jalali et al. described converting a planned peripheral buckle to vitrectomy after identifying detached ICM and breaks that implicated coloboma.

document_sections.heading: Surgical procedure
document_sections.content: The subsequent subsections address encirclage, sclerotomy placement, lens management, vitrectomy, evaluation of the lesion boundary, PVR, retinal reattachment, retinopexy, and tamponade in coloboma-related RD.

document_sections.heading: Role of additional encirclage
document_sections.content: An encircling band offers no definite advantage for a large lesion reaching the inferior periphery. More complete peripheral vitrectomy in aphakic and pseudophakic eyes further reduces its role. With substantial PVR, however, encirclage assists overall traction relief.

document_sections.heading: Sclerotomies
document_sections.content: More anterior sclerotomies might seem appropriate in microphthalmic eyes, but microphthalmos must be distinguished from isolated microcornea. When microcornea occurs without microphthalmos, the distance from limbus to ora is greater than normal.

document_sections.heading: Management of lens
document_sections.content: Besides cataractous lenses, an otherwise clear lens sometimes must be removed when microphthalmos is substantial. A vitrector can remove the lens in most cases, but the dense nuclear sclerosis that is not uncommon with choroidal coloboma may require a phaco fragmatome.

document_sections.heading: Vitrectomy
document_sections.content: In most coloboma-related RDs, posterior vitreous remains attached despite partial vitreous liquefaction in front of the lesion. PVD induction can be difficult, and routine triamcinolone injection is recommended to assist it. If suction with the cutter does not induce PVD, forceps can initiate a detachment pocket near the disc before suction is applied. Scleral indentation assists removal of peripheral vitreous.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of coloboma margin
document_sections.content: Operating-microscope magnification provides a more definite assessment of whether ICM is detached, how far detachment extends, and whether membrane breaks are present.

document_sections.heading: Approach in eyes with significant PVR
document_sections.content: Membrane peeling resembles that in other PVR cases. If a retinotomy is required to remove a sub-retinal band, it should be placed as far peripherally as possible because coloboma occupies inferior fundus and available functional retina superiorly is limited.

document_sections.heading: Retinal reattachment
document_sections.content: Fluid air exchange without direct sub-retinal fluid removal can reveal the route of fluid movement and the underlying detachment mechanism.

document_sections.heading: Situation 1
document_sections.content: With ICM breaks and breaks at the zone of least resistance, with or without peripheral breaks, injected air pushes subretinal fluid into the vitreous cavity through ICM breaks. Positioning the suction port over the coloboma can therefore flatten retina without a drainage retinotomy. If communication between sub-retinal and sub-ICM spaces is too narrow, especially with thick fluid, drainage may be slow and the retina may temporarily balloon as in Situation 2. Continued fluid accumulation on the lesion floor during aspiration, together with gradual reduction of surrounding bullous RD, distinguishes this circumstance.

document_sections.heading: Situation 2
document_sections.content: If a peripheral break is present without a defect in the zone of least resistance, injected air leaves sub-retinal fluid without an exit. Fluid accumulates around the lesion edge and balloons the retina; flattening requires aspiration through an existing peripheral break or creation of a drainage retinotomy.

document_sections.heading: Situation 3
document_sections.content: This comparatively rare combination comprises a peripheral break and a defect at the site of least resistance but no ICM break. During fluid air exchange, both retina and its connected ICM detachment balloon rather than flatten.

document_sections.heading: Retinopexy
document_sections.content: For RD unrelated to coloboma, retinopexy is, strictly, needed only around peripheral retinal breaks. Coloboma-related RD requires treatment at the lesion edge to close communications in the zone of least resistance. Treating only a known communicating segment would theoretically suffice, but its position is usually unknown and PVD induction may create further tears; treatment of the entire coloboma margin is therefore advised. When pars plana surgery treats an unrelated RD, preventive treatment of that margin may also be preferable. Treatment of extra-colobomatous ora serrata is optional and aims to reduce recurrence from unrecognized ora dialysis, particularly near sclerotomy meridians.

document_sections.heading: Role of relaxing incisions in the ICM
document_sections.content: A taut ICM containing breaks over deep ectasia can lift like a trampoline, allowing air to enter beneath it during fluid air exchange even when adjacent retina settles. This traction might prevent laser-induced adhesion at the lesion edge. If necessary, relaxing ICM cuts can relieve traction, but major vessels crossing the membrane to supply retina beyond it must be avoided.

document_sections.heading: Difficulties in performing retinopexy along coloboma margin
document_sections.content: A tense ICM may obstruct laser placement directly at the boundary and require wider treatment. If the fovea lies immediately outside that boundary, wider treatment could destroy it; sparing the fovea by treating on either side leaves a possible site of communication between sub-retinal and sub-ICM spaces and a risk of recurrent RD after oil removal. If the disc participates in the defect, light burns must be placed carefully around the functional boundary to avoid nerve-fibre damage. Diode laser can help prevent unintended full-thickness burns.

document_sections.heading: Internal tamponade
document_sections.content: Silicone oil provides desirable long-term tamponade in most cases because patients are often young and difficult to position reliably, while the area requiring support is large and extends below the horizontal meridian on both sides. C3F8 may be acceptable in selected cases. For silicone oil, 5000 centistokes may be preferable: low-viscosity oil could emulsify more readily in highly active children through mechanical agitation.

document_sections.heading: Results of management of coloboma-related RD
document_sections.content: Hanneken reported successful outcomes in seven out of eight eyes after pars plana vitrectomy. In Gopal et al.'s series of 85 eyes, silicone oil tamponade was used in 94.1% eyes and C3F8 in 5.9% eyes; oil was removed in 80% eyes after an average duration of 4.7 months. Overall success was 81.17%. Re-detachment affected 16 eyes: 3 out of 5 eyes treated with C3F8 and 13 out of 80 eyes treated with silicone oil. Raised intraocular pressure occurred in 16% of eyes. Pal et al. reported 88.1% success among 40 eyes; recurrent RD followed oil removal in ten of the 21 eyes undergoing removal. Nagpal et al. reported 88.9% success in 46 eyes, of which 38 underwent vitrectomy with silicone oil and 8 underwent scleral buckling. A multicentric retrospective study of 119 eyes reported final anatomical success of 87.4%; tamponade was silicone oil in 77.3% eyes, SF6 in 10.1%, and C3F8 in 12.6%. SF6 was associated with 50% recurrence risk, or 6 out of 12 eyes. These findings suggest that a pars plana approach with silicone oil is probably necessary in a majority of cases. Despite anatomical success rates of more than 80%, acuity better than 20/400 was reported in only 35.7–78.4% cases; disc and macular involvement explain the discrepancy between anatomical and visual outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Post-silicone oil removal risk of recurrent RD
document_sections.content: Concern about recurrent RD can delay oil removal and thereby increase oil-induced complications. Possible causes of recurrence include incomplete vitrectomy or failure to induce PVD, leaving unrecognized traction that becomes evident after removal; missed ora dialysis near sclerotomies; overlooked shallow RD outside the treated coloboma margin, potentially indicating persistent sub-ICM to sub-retinal communication; and proliferative vitreo retinopathy. Pre-operative OCT, when feasible, can help detect shallow detachment, and intra-operative OCT could have a role. A taut ICM often causes such shallow detachment; broader laser, when feasible, helps reduce recurrence. Careful intraoperative examination of the whole retina, including the lesion edge, during oil removal provides an opportunity to correct problems immediately, including reinjection of silicone oil when necessary.

document_sections.heading: Choroidal neovascularization (CNV)
document_sections.content: Sub foveal CNV has been reported when the macula lies near a choroidal coloboma boundary. The membrane is usually classic and may be pigmented. Reported treatments include laser photocoagulation, photodynamic therapy with Verteporfin, anti VEGF injections, and surgical membrane removal.

document_sections.heading: Scleral fistula
document_sections.content: Thin, ectatic sclera may rupture spontaneously or after minor trauma and form a fistula. Reported repairs include fibrin glue, a scleral patch graft, and a buckle; spontaneous closure has also been reported in one case. Affected eyes present with low IOP and signs of hypotony maculopathy.

document_sections.heading: Cataract
document_sections.content: Uveal coloboma is associated with early cataract, often substantial nuclear opacity even at a young age. In Mohamed et al.'s series of 145 eyes from 98 patients with mean age of 23 years, 48.9% had cataract; nuclear sclerosis was the commonest opacity, at 51%. A linear opacity in the coloboma region occurred in 29% of cases and was termed ‘coloboma cataract’. Lens dislocation or subluxation occurred in a few eyes. Cataract surgery has been reported to have increased complications. Chaurasia et al. operated on 26 eyes, using phaco emulsification for softer or moderately hard lenses and extra capsular cataract surgery for very hard lenses; intra-operative complications in 8/26 eyes comprised rhexis extension, posterior capsule rupture, and vitreous loss. Phylactou et al. reported posterior capsule tear with vitreous loss in 19.5%. Khokhar et al. successfully treated 21 eyes using phaco emulsification and IOL implantation assisted by capsular and iris hooks; nuclei were hard and leathery, and they recommend placing haptics perpendicular to the coloboma for improved centration. Kohli et al. reported complications in 9.3% of a series of 280 eyes undergoing phaco emulsification or manual small incisional cataract surgery (MSICS). They recommend phaco emulsification for softer cataracts when corneal diameter is >8 mm and M-SICS for smaller corneas with hard nuclear cataracts. For extremely microphthalmic eyes, a pars plana approach is recommended even for hard lenses because a small cornea makes limbal surgery difficult.

document_sections.heading: Repair of iris coloboma along with cataract surgery
document_sections.content: Concurrent iris-coloboma repair has been reported with the stated aim of reducing postoperative glare. Khokhar et al. reported no postoperative complaints of glare or diplopia despite not repairing the iris. Because affected patients have had the iris defect since birth and are accustomed to any associated glare, repair, if undertaken, is considered more cosmetic than functional.

document_sections.heading: Prophylaxis against RD in eyes with coloboma of choroid
document_sections.content: Lifetime RD risk makes prevention important, but preventive laser raises questions of completeness and safety. Effective isolation of a coloboma from surrounding retina requires at least 2–3 rows of burns around its entire boundary. This can be performed safely only when disc and macula are not involved and there is sufficient distance from both to the lesion border; in a majority of affected eyes, the disc lies within the coloboma. With disc involvement, treatment near its functional edge risks nerve-fibre injury from heavy burns. Burn intensity is less precisely controlled by indirect ophthalmoscopy than by slit lamp, yet children under anaesthesia can receive only indirect ophthalmoscopic delivery. Tripathi et al. reported preventive laser in 201 eyes followed for 3 years and described four treatment patterns. In three patterns, sectors were spared to protect the macula; an untreated sector could contain a connection between sub-ICM and sub-retinal spaces and undermine prevention. Two eyes developed RD despite laser during 3 years. In Uhumwangho et al.'s series, mean follow-up was 1.59 years in treatment naïve patients versus 0.79 years in lasertreated patients. Neither study establishes efficacy because follow-up was short relative to RD risk, which accumulates with age. Complete treatment, where feasible, should substantially lower RD risk, but whether partial treatment has preventive value remains unresolved without long-term studies.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: Ocular coloboma has widely varying presentations. Inherited and chromosomally associated forms are described, but sporadic cases are more common; environmental and maternal factors probably contribute to these. The lesion itself can impair vision by involving the disc or fovea, and complications including RD or choroidal neovascularisation can also reduce vision. Detecting ICM detachment is essential to assess whether coloboma contributes to RD. Pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil and endolaser along the lesion edge is associated with good surgical success. Cataract surgery carries a higher-than-usual complication risk. Proposed research priorities are better identification of causes of non-syndromic coloboma; wider-field anatomical assessment through longer swept source OCT scans; randomized controlled trials of preventive laser photocoagulation for RD; and randomized controlled trials comparing internal tamponades for coloboma-related RD.
